title: Generative AI Enhances Individual Creativity but Reduces the Collective Diversity of Novel Content
author: Anil R. Doshi · Oliver P. Hauser

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s outcome-specific evidence into open-ended literary creativity: GenAI improved story novelty and usefulness, with larger gains for less creative writers. This materially strengthens the finding that assisted performance gaps can narrow, while offering no evidence about employment, income, durable learning or career outcomes.
qs: We find that having access to GenAI causally increases the average novelty and usefulness—two frequently studied dimensions of creativity—relative to human writers on their own.

However, the gains from writing more creative stories benefit some more than others: less creative writers experience greater uplifts for their stories, seeing increases of 10% to 11% for creativity and of 22% to 26% for how enjoyable and well written the story is.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s measurement-focused approach by providing a randomized unaided-versus-GenAI storytelling design and blinded, multi-evaluator assessment of creativity-related outcomes. It contributes methodology rather than findings, so it does not establish whether AI improves individual creativity or reduces collective diversity.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study reinforces selective, human–AI deployment by showing bounded creativity gains concentrated among lower-baseline performers, while adding a material system-level trade-off: AI-assisted outputs become more homogeneous. It extends the cluster beyond legal work without establishing general competence, autonomy or legal-sector organisational value.
qs: In short, the Human with 5 AI Ideas condition effectively equalizes the creativity scores across less and more creative writers.

Our results show that having access to GenAI ideas ^Lmakes a story more similar to the average of other stories within the same condition (Human with 1 GenAI idea b=0.871, p<0.001; Human with 5 GenAI ideas b=0.718, p=0.003).

st.t: Assisted performance: Gains vary by skill measure
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s caution against treating positive coefficients as evidence of uniform performance gains. Its truncated table reports positive estimates for access to five GenAI ideas, but missing outcome headings, comparison categories and significance definitions prevent substantive interpretation, including any conclusion about quality or collective diversity.

st.t: Creative assistance: Planned test proves no gains
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: the supplied material is a preregistered design for testing AI-assisted human story creation, with prespecified outcomes and analyses, rather than evidence of creativity gains or reduced collective diversity. It also supports the cluster’s characterization of AI as an idea-generation aid rather than an autonomous replacement.

st.t: Creative diversity: Individual gains can homogenise groups
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: GPT-4 starting ideas improved evaluated individual story novelty and usefulness while increasing similarity among AI-assisted stories. It also appropriately limits broader claims by treating publishing-wide convergence and effects under richer interaction as extrapolations rather than demonstrated findings.
qs: We find that the provision of AI ideas improves the story’s novelty by 6.7% (b=0.259, p=0.001, see Table S3; compared to the Human only mean of 3.85) and its usefulness by 6.4% (b=0.319, p<0.001; compared to the Human only mean of 5.02).
However, GenAI-enabled stories are more similar to each other than stories by humans alone.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source indirectly supports the cluster’s core account of AI as a complement that can improve bounded human tasks without demonstrating wholesale replacement or general autonomy. Its finding of larger gains for less-creative users also aligns with heterogeneous user effects, though evidence from nonprofessional creative writing does not directly establish legal-workflow, verification or competence risks.
qs: We focus on the potential complementarities of AI on human creative production.
That said, our results suggest that GenAI may have the largest impact on individuals who are less creative.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s conditional account: GenAI raises average creativity and may disproportionately benefit less-creative users in this specific task, while warning that individual gains can reduce collective output diversity. Its qualified language and limited sample do not support a universal claim that weaker users always gain most.
qs: That said, our results suggest that GenAI may have the largest impact on individuals who are less creative.

Specifically, if the publishing (and self-publishing) industry were to embrace more GenAI-inspired stories, our findings suggest that the produced stories would become less unique in aggregate and more similar to each other—an effect that may be heightened over time, as many GenAI models use the existing corpus of text

kp.k: Randomized experiment tests AI-assisted short-story creation
kp.d: This cross-domain study examines creative writing, not legal services. In a pre-registered online experiment, 293 writers produced eight-sentence stories, with 95 assigned to Human only, 100 to access one GPT-4 idea, and 98 to access up to five ideas. Topics were adventures on the open seas, in the jungle, or on another planet. A separate group of 600 evaluators provided 3,519 retained evaluations, assessing creativity before disclosure of AI assistance. Participants were UK-based Prolific users, not selected for professional writing or publishing experience.
qs: Participants are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: Human only, Human with 1 GenAI idea, and Human with 5 GenAI ideas
A total of 293 stories are collected and then passed to evaluators.
Evaluators read six randomly selected stories without being informed about writers being randomly assigned to access GenAI in some conditions (or not).

kp.k: Access to AI ideas improves evaluated creativity
kp.d: Combining both AI-access conditions, the authors report increases in evaluator-rated novelty of 6.7% (b=0.259, p=0.001; Human only mean 3.85) and usefulness of 6.4% (b=0.319, p<0.001; Human only mean 5.02). Novelty averages assessments of whether stories are novel, original and rare; usefulness averages appropriateness, feasibility and publishability. These are reader evaluations of creative outputs, not demonstrated commercial success or a measured change in writers' underlying abilities.
qs: We find that evaluators assess that stories composed by writers in the two GenAI conditions are more creative, in terms of both novelty and usefulness
Our novelty index has three components (novel, original, and rare), with which we create an average value.
The usefulness index also has three components (appropriate, feasible, and publishable), with which we also create an average value.

kp.k: Greater idea availability produces larger measured gains
kp.d: Access to one idea increased novelty by 5.4% (b=0.207, p=0.021) and usefulness by 3.7% (b=0.185, p=0.039), relative to Human only. Access to up to five ideas increased novelty by 8.1% (b=0.311, p<0.001) and usefulness by 9.0% (b=0.453, p<0.001). Usefulness was 5.1% higher in the five-idea condition than in the one-idea condition (p=0.0012). These estimates concern randomized access, not compulsory consumption: 88.4% of eligible writers requested an idea; in the five-idea condition, the average number requested was 2.55, and 24.5% requested all five.
qs: Across the two GenAI conditions, 88.4% participants choose to call upon GenAI at least once to provide an initial story idea.
When given the option to call upon GenAI more than once in the Human with 5 GenAI ideas condition, participants did so on average 2.55 times, with 24.5% requesting the maximum of five GenAI ideas.
The overall results suggest that having access to more AI ideas lead to more creative storytelling.

kp.k: Reader enjoyment improves without corresponding writer self-assessment changes
kp.d: Exploratory analyses found higher enjoyment and more plot twists in both AI-access conditions. With access to five ideas, stories were also rated better written (b=0.372, p<0.001), more influential on expectations of future stories (b=0.251, p=0.005), and less boring (b=−0.200, p=0.049). There was no statistically significant improvement in humor. Writers' own assessments showed no significant differences across conditions in novelty, usefulness or story characteristics.
qs: Stories in the Human with 5 GenAI ideas are, however, not evaluated as more funny than Human only; if anything the coefficient is negative but not significant
In contrast, writers self-assessing their own stories showed no significant differences in the novelty and usefulness between authors who were offered GenAI ideas and those who were not
Again, writers’ self-assessment of their own stories showed no significant differences in the story characteristics across conditions

kp.k: Lower-creativity writers benefit most from AI assistance
kp.d: Baseline creativity was measured using the Divergent Association Task (DAT), successfully scored for 291 writers, with a mean of 77.24 and standard deviation of 6.48. The authors found no differences in AI access by baseline creativity. Among low-DAT writers, access to one and five ideas improved novelty by 6.3% and 10.7%, and usefulness by 5.5% and 11.5%, respectively. In the five-idea condition, low-DAT writers' ratings rose by up to 26.6% for writing quality and 22.6% for enjoyment, while boredom declined by up to 15.2%. High-DAT writers gained little; the authors interpret the five-idea condition as equalizing evaluated creativity.
qs: Among the most inherently creative writers (i.e., high- DAT writers), there is little effect of having access to GenAI ideas on the creativity of their stories.
In short, we do not observe any differences in how GenAI was accessed based on the inherent creativity of the writer.
In short, the Human with 5 AI Ideas condition effectively equalizes the creativity scores across less and more creative writers.

kp.k: AI assistance anchors stories and reduces collective diversity
kp.d: Using OpenAI embeddings and cosine similarity multiplied by 100, the authors found that stories in the one- and five-idea conditions were respectively 5.2% (b=4.29, p<0.001) and 5.0% (b=4.11, p<0.001) more similar to AI ideas than Human only stories. For writers without generated ideas, the comparison used randomly assigned ideas from the same topic; for users, it used the first generated idea. Stories were also more similar to the average embedding of other stories in their condition: b=0.871 (p<0.001) for one idea and b=0.718 (p=0.003) for five. Thus, higher individual creativity ratings coexisted with reduced diversity across outputs.
qs: In short, writers in the two GenAI conditions are anchored to some extent on the GenAI idea presented to them.
Our results show that having access to GenAI ideas
makes a story more similar to the average of other stories within the same condition

kp.k: AI disclosure lowers perceived human ownership
kp.d: After disclosure of AI availability and use, with generated ideas shown when used, evaluators attributed 25.4% less ownership to writers offered one idea (b=−1.96, p<0.001) and 31.0% less to those offered five (b=−2.40, p<0.001), relative to the Human only ownership-index mean of 7.74. Among stories whose writers requested AI ideas, the five-idea condition reduced hypothetical writer profit allocation by 2.30 percentage points relative to one idea (p=0.072); this difference was not statistically significant after controlling for perceived ownership. These findings concern evaluator beliefs, not legal ownership or actual revenue distributions.
qs: Figure 4A shows that, for stories that were produced by writers who had access to GenAI, evaluators attribute substantially less ownership to the writer.

Furthermore, this weak relationship is no longer statistically significant when we include as a control variable the extent to which the evaluator ascribes ownership of the story to the writer in both conditions.

kp.k: Readers accept AI ideation but favor acknowledgment
kp.d: In exploratory attitude questions, 52.7% disagreed that AI-assisted story writing is unethical, versus 35.7% agreeing; 54.5% disagreed that any AI use negates a creative act, versus 33.8% agreeing. Initial-idea assistance was acceptable to 58.7%, while 26.5% disagreed. However, 70.2% rejected using AI to write an entire story without acknowledgment, versus 20.2% accepting it. Compensation for creators of underlying content attracted 51.7% agreement, and making AI-generated inputs accessible alongside the final story attracted 46.7% agreement. These figures describe this evaluator sample's attitudes, not regulatory requirements.
qs: However, according to evaluators, there were limits in the acceptability of the use of AI.
It is ethically acceptable to use AI to write an entire story without acknowledging the use of AI.
There was also consensus that the content creators on which the AI output was based ought to be compensated

kp.k: Findings concern constrained augmentation rather than autonomous replacement
kp.d: The authors study human–AI complementarity: GPT-4 supplied three-sentence starting ideas through fixed prompts, while humans wrote the stories. Writers could neither customize prompts nor converse iteratively with the model, and could not copy and paste idea text. The reported causal interpretation is based on intention-to-treat analysis of randomized availability regardless of uptake. Professional writers and unusually creative individuals were not studied. The suggestion that more interactive assistance could yield greater benefits is conditional speculation, not an experimentally established result.
qs: We focus on the potential complementarities of AI on human creative production.

We do not allow writers to customize the call to the GenAI engine, nor do we allow for repeated interactions between writers and GenAI, both of which may increase the effectiveness and magnitude of the impact of GenAI on creativity.
Participants were not able to copy and paste the GenAI idea text.
we do not study professional writers or unusually creative individuals.

kp.k: Widespread adoption could amplify homogenization over time
kp.d: The authors caution that broader publishing and self-publishing adoption could make stories less unique in aggregate. They hypothesize that training future models on an increasingly AI-influenced corpus could heighten this reduction in diversity, citing separate research on instability in models trained on generated content. The experiment itself does not test industry-wide adoption, repeated training cycles or long-term outcomes. The authors also report no evidence that AI ideas raised creativity beyond the performance of particularly creative humans, and recommend research involving deeper interaction and specialized tools.
qs: Specifically, if the publishing (and self-publishing) industry were to embrace more GenAI-inspired stories, our findings suggest that the produced stories would become less unique in aggregate and more similar to each other
Initial evidence suggests that GenAI models trained with GenAI content become unstable (33).

We do not find evidence of this possibility in this study; however, to test this hypothesis more thoroughly, we encourage future research to allow creatives to engage with GenAI more deeply and interactively, and to extend this work by leveraging more specialized GenAI tools for this purpose.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Doshi and Hauser find that access to GPT-4 story ideas improves reader-rated creativity and several aspects of writing quality; this is a claim about creative writing, not legal services.
pts.d: Combining the two AI-access conditions, the authors report increases of 6.7% in novelty and 6.4% in usefulness relative to human-only writing. Access to one idea increased novelty by 5.4% and usefulness by 3.7%; access to up to five increased them by 8.1% and 9.0%. Usefulness includes appropriateness for the audience and potential development into a publishable book, rather than actual sales or publication. Exploratory reader assessments found AI-assisted stories more enjoyable and more likely to contain plot twists; the five-idea condition also improved assessments of writing quality and reduced boredom. There was no significant improvement in humor. Writers' own assessments did not show significant differences across conditions.

pts.k: The authors find that gains are concentrated among writers with lower baseline creativity, narrowing differences in assessed output.
pts.d: Baseline creativity was operationalized using the Divergent Association Task (DAT). For low-DAT writers, access to one or five ideas increased assessed novelty by 6.3% or 10.7% and usefulness by 5.5% or 11.5%, respectively. In the five-idea condition, reported improvements reached 26.6% for writing quality and 22.6% for enjoyment, with boredom decreasing by up to 15.2%. High-DAT writers showed little benefit. The authors describe the five-idea condition as effectively equalizing creativity scores; they do not find evidence that AI raises output beyond what the most creative participants could produce unaided.

pts.k: Improved individual stories coexist with reduced collective diversity and anchoring on AI-generated ideas.
pts.d: The authors report that stories in the one-idea and five-idea conditions were respectively 5.2% and 5.0% more similar to AI ideas than human-only stories. Similarity to the average embedding of other stories within the same condition increased by 0.871 and 0.718 points on the authors' 100-scaled cosine-similarity measure. They interpret this as evidence of anchoring and greater similarity across AI-assisted outputs, notwithstanding higher reader-rated novelty of individual stories.

pts.k: AI involvement reduces readers' attribution of ownership to writers, while readers generally accept AI ideation but expect acknowledgement.
pts.d: After disclosure of AI access and use, with generated ideas shown where applicable, evaluators attributed 25.4% less ownership to writers offered one idea and 31.0% less to those offered up to five. These are perceived ownership claims, not determinations of copyright law. Among stories for which AI was used, the five-idea condition attracted a 2.30-percentage-point lower hypothetical writer profit share than the one-idea condition; this was only marginally significant and ceased to be significant after controlling for perceived ownership. In exploratory attitude questions, 58.7% accepted AI use for an initial idea, 70.2% rejected writing an entire story using AI without acknowledgement, and 51.7% supported compensating creators whose content underlay AI output. These are respondents' preferences, not legal requirements or observed market payments.

pts.k: The authors predict conditionally that widespread AI-assisted publishing could homogenize content, potentially increasingly over time.
pts.d: Extrapolating from their similarity results, Doshi and Hauser suggest that publishing and self-publishing would produce less collectively unique stories if they broadly embraced AI-generated starting ideas. They further propose that training subsequent models on an increasingly AI-influenced text corpus could intensify diversity loss. This is a downstream scenario without a specified date or adoption threshold, not an observed publishing-market or longitudinal result. The authors cite external initial evidence of instability in models trained on generated content, alongside their own experiment. They also suggest that professional creatives might gain efficiency or speed, but identify those populations as unstudied here.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main findings derive from a preregistered randomized online writing experiment, separate reader evaluations, and embedding-based similarity analysis.
pts.d: The analyzed sample comprises 293 UK Prolific writers assigned to human-only writing (95), access to one GPT-4 idea (100), or access to up to five ideas (98). A separate group of 600 UK evaluators provided 3,519 retained story evaluations; initial creativity ratings preceded disclosure of AI involvement. Novelty and usefulness were preregistered indices measured on nine-point scales. The authors used OLS, robust standard errors for writer-level outcomes, and evaluator-clustered standard errors for reader outcomes, with additional fixed-effects robustness checks. Of those offered AI access, 88.4% requested at least one idea. The causal estimand is access to ideas, using intention-to-treat analysis, rather than the effect of compulsory use or each additional idea actually requested. DAT interactions support the heterogeneous-effects claims. OpenAI embeddings and cosine similarity support the diversity findings; first-generated ideas were used for AI users and randomly allocated topic-matched ideas for nonusers. Ownership and profit findings are survey-based assessments following disclosure.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Observed effects concern a single constrained writing exercise using GPT-4; professional, interactive, and longer-term effects remain untested.
pts.d: The 2024 source measures immediate output from eight-sentence English adventure stories intended for readers approximately aged 15–24, across three assigned topics. AI supplied three-sentence starting ideas through fixed prompts, with no prompt customization or conversational iteration. Writers could request ideas but still composed the final story; this tests augmentation rather than autonomous replacement. Participants were not selected as professional writers or unusually creative individuals, and evaluators were ordinary readers rather than publishing professionals. The authors acknowledge population-representativeness limits and rapid model change. They speculate conditionally that more interactive or customized access could produce greater gains, making these estimates a possible lower bound; this is not experimentally established. The study does not establish lasting changes in writers' underlying ability, professional productivity, employment, or legal-service outcomes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source concerns ordinary writers, readers, publishing participants, and creators associated with AI inputs—not lawyers or legal-service buyers.
pts.d: Lower-DAT writers receive the largest measured benefits, while higher-DAT writers retain strong performance with little added gain. Readers rate assisted stories more highly on several dimensions but encounter more similar outputs in aggregate and assign writers less ownership after disclosure. Publishers and self-publishers are the subjects of the conditional homogenization prediction. Writers and AI-tool creators are potential recipients of hypothetical profit allocations; creators of underlying content are subjects of respondents' compensation preferences. Researchers, policymakers, and practitioners are addressed as audiences concerned with creativity and over-reliance. No direct claims are made about law firms, legal departments, legal staffing, legal pricing, access to justice, or legal work quality.
